scope: Princely-state events outside the Company / Crown direct-rule provinces — Bhopal, Hyderabad, Travancore, Mysore (post-Tipu), Kashmir, the Rajputana states. Seeded with Sultan Jahan Begum's autobiography.

events.title: Sultan Jahan Begum writes Akhtar-i-Iqbal
events.tooltip: Sultan Jahan Begum publishes Persian memoir, Bhopal, 1912
events.summary: Last of four successive Begum-rulers of Bhopal writes a Persian memoir and three-volume English autobiography — first-person record of a sovereign woman.
events.detail: Sultan Jahan Begum (1858–1930), the fourth of four successive Begum-rulers of Bhopal across more than a century, published the Persian Akhtar-i-Iqbal (1912) and dictated the three-volume English autobiography An Account of My Life between 1910 and 1927. Bhopal was unique among princely states for matrilineal female succession (Qudsia Begum from 1819 → Sikandar → Shah Jahan → Sultan Jahan, who abdicated 1926). The memoirs document the politics of being a Muslim ruling woman within colonial paramountcy, the founding of Sultania Girls' School (1903), her presidency of the All-India Muslim Ladies' Conference, the Aligarh women's college (Sultan Jahan was its first chancellor, 1920), and her rupture with her son Hamidullah Khan over the abdication terms. Among the few autobiographies by an Indian ruling sovereign in any era; the only such by a Muslim woman.

date.display: Akhtar-i-Iqbal published 1912; An Account of My Life vols. 1910–1927

sources.label: Sultan Jahan Begum, An Account of My Life (3 vols., 1910–1927; vol. 1 trans. C.H. Payne, John Murray)
Shaharyar M. Khan, The Begums of Bhopal: A Dynasty of Women Rulers in Raj India (2000)
Siobhan Lambert-Hurley, Muslim Women, Reform and Princely Patronage: Nawab Sultan Jahan Begam of Bhopal (2007)

events.title: Telangana Rebellion
events.tooltip: Communist-led peasant rebellion in the Nizam's domain, 1946–1951
events.summary: CPI-led peasants and tribals seized 3,000 villages from doras across Hyderabad — continued past the 1948 Indian annexation against the Nehru government.
events.detail: The Telangana Rebellion began in July 1946 in the Nalgonda and Warangal districts of the Nizam of Hyderabad's domain, against the dora landlord system — vetti (forced unpaid labour) extracted from peasants and tribals (Lambadas, Koyas) under cover of the princely state's near-feudal land laws. The Andhra Mahasabha and the Communist Party of India organised armed peasant squads (dalams) that by 1948 had liberated approximately 3,000 villages across an area of 16,000 square miles, redistributing 1 million acres of land, abolishing vetti and debt bondage, and running parallel administration through gram rajyams (village republics). The Nizam's Razakar militia under Qasim Razvi targeted the movement until India's annexation of Hyderabad in September 1948 (Operation Polo). The Indian Army then turned on the Communist movement; suppression continued until October 1951 when the CPI formally withdrew the armed struggle. Roughly 4,000 peasant fighters and supporters killed, 50,000 imprisoned. The movement is the foundational case in modern Indian armed-left politics — direct ancestor of the Naxalbari uprising twenty years later.

sources.label: P. Sundarayya, Telangana People's Struggle and Its Lessons (CPI(M), 1972) — by the movement's principal organiser
